### Entity conventions distilled

- **Tabs for indentation** everywhere (Spring's own style). Blank line between every field.
- `@Entity` + `@Table(name = "…")` always explicit, even where the implicit name matches.
- `@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` on a `private Long id;` — **always a surrogate id**, never a natural/assigned key (Spring Data would then `merge` instead of `insert`).
- **Every enum field gets both** `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` **and** `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)`, with the inline comment `// If left unannotated, JPA stores the status by ordinal. See design decision 29.` The `@JdbcTypeCode` is mandatory or `validate` fails (H2 native `enum` column).
- Timestamps are `java.time.Instant`, **passed in as a constructor parameter**, never `Instant.now()` (the `Clock` bean on `GlobalPaymentServiceApplication` is the one source of now). Field name `createdAt` → column `created_at`.
- `protected NoArgs() { // required by JPA }` — exactly that comment.
- All constructor args guarded by `Objects.requireNonNull(x, "a lowercase domain sentence")`.
- **No setters, ever.** Every state transition is a `@Modifying @Query` guarded update on the repository, with the "a setter would offer a second way … that quietly is not atomic" justification.
- Entity class is **package-private** (`class CheckLedgerEntry`, `class IdempotencyRecord`) unless another slice must name it (`public class Transfer`).
- Repositories extend the **bare `org.springframework.data.repository.Repository`**, never `JpaRepository`/`CrudRepository` — "it declares nothing, so every method here is one with a call site today". Package-private interface. Text blocks for JPQL, uppercase JPQL keywords, `entry`/`transfer` as the alias (not `e`/`t`).
- Javadoc is long, argumentative prose: `<p>` paragraphs, `<b>`/`<em>` for the claim sentence, references to `design decision N`, `ticket N`, and named test classes.

## 4. The other two "public ports" — **neither is built yet**

This is the most important correction to your assumptions. The three ports are named in `docs/design-decisions/00-initial-decisions.md` §30:

```
├── idempotency/   IdempotentExecution (public) · JDBC impl package-private
├── fx/            ExchangeRateProvider (public) · HTTP client package-private
├── outbox/        EventPublisher (public) · OutboxPoller package-private
```
> "The three public ports are exactly §3, §11/§12 and the FX client"

**None of the three types exists on disk.** `fx/` contains only `CurrencyConversion.java`, `ConversionResult.java`, `package-info.java` — the port arrives with ticket 25. `idempotency/` contains no public type at all; its `package-info.java` says so explicitly:

> "The port design decision 3 describes … is not here yet. It arrives with the first caller that has a use for it, which is the duplicate resolution of ticket 17."

Likewise §30's ticket-16 amendment: *"the slice ships the storage under the port and not the port itself … Nothing in the package is public, so the line's `IdempotentExecution (public)` is what ticket 17 makes true."*

**So `EventPublisher` will be the first of the three ports actually written.** The shapes to copy from instead:

### a) The public-facade-over-package-private-internals shape — `transfers/checks/CheckLedger.java`

The single closest precedent. `@Component`, **public class with public methods** (because `@Transactional` on non-public is silently ignored), package-private constructor, package-private collaborators:

```java
@Component
public class CheckLedger {

	private final CheckPolicy policy;

	private final CheckLedgerRepository entries;

	CheckLedger(CheckPolicy policy, CheckLedgerRepository entries) {
		this.policy = policy;
		this.entries = entries;
	}

	@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
	public void openFor(Transfer transfer) { … }
```

with the visibility rationale stated in its Javadoc:

> "The method is public on a package-private-by-default design because `@Transactional` on a non-public method is silently ignored under proxy-based AOP — the trap `hu.bankmonitor.payments` documents. The class is public for the ordinary reason: `FundsReservation` is in the parent package and has to name it."

Same shape at `accounts/AccountLocking.java` (`@Component public class AccountLocking`, package-private ctor, `@Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY) public LockedAccounts lockForTransfer(...)`).

Note: this codebase uses `@Component` for these facades and `@Service` for the transaction-owning application services (`FundsReservation`, `VerdictRecording`, `IdempotencyClaims` — all `@Service` + package-private class + public `@Transactional` methods). There is **no `@Configuration` bean-method style** except `mockfx/MockExchangeRateProvider` (`@Configuration @Profile(...)` holding a `WebSecurityCustomizer` bean) and the `Clock` bean on the application class.

### b) The interface-with-one-method shape — sealed/enum vocabulary

`fx/ConversionResult.java` is the precedent for a small public interface with Javadoc that says why the shape is what it is; `Check`/`Verdict` are the precedent for public enums that are part of the schema:

> *(Check.java)* "The constants are stored by name, so they are part of the schema: `V4__check_ledger.sql` lists them in a check constraint, and renaming one is a migration rather than a refactor."

### c) `mockfx/FlakinessSettings.java` — the config-properties shape, if the poller gets a configurable interval

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(FlakinessSettings.PREFIX)
@Validated
record FlakinessSettings(
		@DecimalMin("0.0") @DecimalMax("1.0") @DefaultValue("0.3") double failureRate,
		@DefaultValue("200ms") Duration latency) {

	static final String PREFIX = "payments.mock-fx";
}
```
Registered via `@EnableConfigurationProperties(FlakinessSettings.class)` on the slice's `@Configuration`. Defaults live in the record ("so there is one copy of them, and so that the settings cannot be half-absent"), namespace prefix is `payments.<slice>`.

### 5a. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/ModuleBoundariesHoldTest.java` (full, shown above in tool output; the load-bearing parts)

			.that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Controller")
			.or().areMetaAnnotatedWith(Controller.class)
			.should().dependOnClassesThat().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Repository")
			.orShould().dependOnClassesThat().areAssignableTo(Repository.class)
			.because("a controller holding a repository has skipped the service that owns the transaction")
			.allowEmptyShould(true);

				.matching(rootPackage + ".(*)..")
				.should().beFreeOfCycles()
				.allowEmptyShould(true);

Three tests: `everyPackageOfTheDesignExists` (asserts `outbox` is on the classpath — the existing `package-info.java` is what puts it there), `theSlicesAreFreeOfCycles`, `noControllerReachesARepository`. Plus a `@Nested class RulesFailWhenViolated` that runs each rule against deliberate fixtures under `hu.bankmonitor.testsupport.boundaryviolations.*` and asserts the rule *fails*. **Convention: every new prohibition rule ships with a falsification fixture.**

**Implications for ticket 27:**
- `slices().matching("hu.bankmonitor.payments.(*)..")` — `outbox` must not depend on `transfers` (ticket 28 has `transfers` writing outbox rows; the dependency runs one way). Do not import anything from `transfers` into `outbox`.
- No class named `*Controller` or meta-annotated `@Controller` may depend on anything named `*Repository` or assignable to `Repository`. The poller is not a controller, so it's fine.

### 5b. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/transfers/NothingButTheReservationCreatesATransferTest.java` — **the "which classes may write entities" rule**

```java
	private static final ArchRule ONLY_THE_RESERVATION_WRITES_A_TRANSFER = noClasses()
			.that().doNotHaveFullyQualifiedName(FundsReservation.class.getName())
			.should().dependOnClassesThat().haveFullyQualifiedName(TransferRepository.class.getName())
			.because("a Transfer written anywhere else would be PENDING against an empty check ledger");
```

The rule is by **dependency on the interface**, not by call. Its Javadoc names the axis explicitly:

> "So the axis is not read against write … It is restricted against unrestricted. Creating a Transfer is restricted because one written anywhere else would be `PENDING` against an empty Check Ledger; advancing one is not, because the guard travels with the statement."

There is **no analogous rule for outbox rows yet**. If you add one, the established pattern is: a separate `Repository` interface per access kind (`TransferRepository` = write only, `TransferQueries` = reads, `TransferTransitions` = lock + guarded update), each package-private, so that "a reader cannot call `save` because it cannot name it".

### 5c. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/LockedPathTouchesOnlyTheDatabaseTest.java` — the reachability walk

```java
	private static final DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE = resideInAnyPackage(
			"java.net..",
			"java.io..",
			"java.nio.file..",
			"jakarta.servlet..",
			"org.springframework.web..",
			"org.springframework.http..",

**This is the rule ticket 27 can break.** `FundsReservation` and `VerdictRecording` are lock holders; the walk is transitive over application classes. When ticket 28 makes them write outbox events, anything reachable from `EventPublisher` must not touch `java.net`, `java.io`, `org.springframework.web/http`, or the `fx`/`mockfx` packages. A log-line `EventPublisher` is fine; note that the walk stops at interfaces, so a port declared in `outbox` with an impl in `outbox` is walked (both are application classes) — keep the log implementation free of `java.io` (SLF4J is `org.slf4j`, not matched).

`hu.bankmonitor.payments.outbox..` is **not** currently in `IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE`, which is consistent with the outbox being a database write held inside the lock.

## 7. Logging conventions

Only **three** log statements exist in `src/main/java`. There is **no structured/key-value logging library** — no logstash-encoder, no `StructuredArguments`, no `atInfo().addKeyValue()`, no MDC. `grep` for all of those returns nothing. So "a structured log line" means SLF4J parameterised placeholders, not fluent key-value.

The house style:

**Declaration** (always `private static final Logger log`, lowercase `log`, `LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class)`, placed *after* other `static final` constants and *before* instance fields):

```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/DemoAccountSeeder.java:43
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(DemoAccountSeeder.class);
```
```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/mockfx/MockExchangeRateController.java:50
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MockExchangeRateController.class);
```

**Example 1 — info with `{}` placeholders** (`DemoAccountSeeder.java:62`):

```java
	@Override
	public void run(String... args) {
		List<Account> seeded = accounts.saveAll(OPENING_BALANCES.stream().map(Account::new).toList());

		log.info("Seeded {} demo accounts for the '{}' profile", seeded.size(), DEV_PROFILE);
	}
```

**Example 2 — error with the throwable as last arg** (`MockExchangeRateController.java:108`), and note the Javadoc explains *why the line exists*:

```java
	/**
	 * …
	 * <p>It is logged before it is swallowed. The response deliberately says nothing about
	 * what went wrong — a third party's would not — so without this line the one place the
	 * defect could be seen is the place that discards it.
	 */
	@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
	ResponseEntity<ProviderFault> anythingElse(Exception failure) {
		log.error("The stand-in FX provider failed to answer a request", failure);
		return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
				.body(new ProviderFault("rate_service_error", "The rate service failed to answer."));
	}
```

**Example 3 — the one place a different name is used** (`src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/ProblemDocumentAdvice.java:194`), inherited `logger` from `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`, string concatenation:

```java
		logger.error("Unhandled exception, answered as " + ProblemType.INTERNAL_ERROR.urn(), exception);
```

Message style: **sentence case, capital first letter, no trailing period, no prefixes/brackets/tags.** Values interpolated via `{}` (quoted with `'…'` when a string identifier). No log levels below `info` are used anywhere.

import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.server.LocalServerPort;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.client.RestTestClient;

/**
 * Base for tests that need the whole application running on a real port.
 *
 * <p>The configuration lives here rather than being repeated on each subclass for a
 * reason beyond tidiness: Spring caches one application context per distinct
 * configuration, so two classes differing by a single annotation pay two boots. Holding
 * the annotations in one place makes the shared context structural rather than a
 * coincidence the next edit could break.
 *
 * <p>{@code RANDOM_PORT} rather than MockMvc, because the claims these tests make are
 * about the servlet container itself — that a request reaches a listening socket, and
 * what kind of thread Tomcat serves it on. MockMvc would bypass it and prove neither.
 */
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(ThreadProbeController.class)
public abstract class BootedApplicationTest {

	@LocalServerPort
	private int port;

	/**
	 * A client bound to the running server. {@code TestRestTemplate} is gone in Spring
	 * Boot 4; {@code RestTestClient} is its Spring Framework 7 replacement.
	 */
	protected RestTestClient client() {
		return RestTestClient.bindToServer().baseUrl("http://localhost:" + port).build();
	}
}

```sql
create table check_ledger (
    id             bigint generated by default as identity primary key,

    transfer_id    bigint      not null,

    -- `check` is reserved in SQL, so the entity's field is `requiredCheck`. See 19-check-ledger-and-policy.md.
    required_check varchar(15) not null,

    -- Nullable on purpose: no Verdict is how the table says this Check has not answered yet.
    verdict        varchar(8),

    constraint check_ledger_transfer
        foreign key (transfer_id) references transfers (id),

    -- The ledger is fixed when the Transfer is written, not a log of what was reported.
    constraint check_ledger_one_row_per_check
        unique (transfer_id, required_check),

    -- `= any (array[…])`, never `in (…)` — the README beside this file has why.
    constraint check_ledger_check_is_known
        check (required_check = any (array['FRAUD', 'MANUAL_APPROVAL'])),
    constraint check_ledger_verdict_is_known
        check (verdict is null or verdict = any (array['APPROVED', 'REJECTED']))
);

### Extracted dialect/style rules

- **All lowercase SQL keywords.** Column names left-aligned, types aligned in a column, blank lines grouping related columns.
- **Id:** `id bigint generated by default as identity primary key` — verbatim in all four migrations. `generated by default` (not `always`) is load-bearing: tests insert explicit ids (`TransferScenario.openAccount`).
- **Timestamp:** `timestamp(6) with time zone not null` (only occurrence, `transfers.created_at`, maps to `java.time.Instant`).
- **Enum-backed columns:** `varchar(N)` where N is the longest constant, plus a named `check … = any (array[…])`. `varchar(15)` for `MANUAL_APPROVAL`, `varchar(8)` for `REJECTED`/`APPROVED`, `varchar(11)` for `IN_PROGRESS`.
- **Constraint naming:** `<table>_<what_it_says>`, snake_case, no `chk_`/`fk_` prefixes — `transfers_status_is_known`, `check_ledger_one_row_per_check`, `idempotency_records_response_only_when_succeeded`, `check_ledger_transfer` (FK).
- **`in (…)` is forbidden in check constraints** — H2 folds it into a session-ordered set and every later insert fails. Always `col = any (array[…])`; nullable columns take `col is null or col = any (array[…])`.
- **Comments:** `--` lines *above* the thing, stating the non-obvious *why*, often ending with a pointer to `NN-<ticket>.md`. No comment restates a column name.
- **No index exists anywhere in the codebase yet.** `grep -i index src/main/resources/db/migration src/main/java` returns only an unrelated `step.getIndex()`. Ticket 27's unsent index will be the first, so there is no index naming precedent — but §29 anticipates it:

> *(00-initial-decisions.md ~line 1029)* "the natural home for the indexes the design implies: the outbox poller's `WHERE sent_at IS NULL`, the reaper's `WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND deadline < ?`."

The constraint convention (`<table>_<what>`) is the only naming precedent to extend, e.g. `outbox_events_unsent`.

### `db/migration/README.md` (full)

```markdown
# Migrations

Flyway owns this schema. `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` is on, so Hibernate
checks the entities against whatever these files produced and never generates DDL itself.
A mismatch is a startup failure naming the table or column it could not find.

## One migration per slice

Each ticket that introduces a table or a column ships the migration for it, in the same
commit as the entity: `V1__accounts.sql`, `V2__transfers.sql`, and so on, including the
later ones that only add a column. Do not write ahead of the entities — a migration for a
table nothing maps yet is the one artefact `validate` cannot check while you are writing
it.

Numbers are global and never reused. Applied migrations are immutable: to change
something a released migration created, add the next `V`.

## Invariants belong here too

`V1__accounts.sql` carries named `check` constraints, and they are not a substitute for
the domain check above them — an overdraft has to be refused in the service, under the
lock, to reach the caller as a `422` rather than a constraint violation. What the
constraint adds is that a path *around* that check fails the write. Name them, so a
violation says which rule was broken.

Hand-written constraints are fine under `validate`. The trouble design decision 29 records
is with Hibernate's *schema export* emitting one under `create-drop`, which is a setting
this application never uses.

## Seed data does not go here

A migration runs everywhere Flyway runs, the test suite included, so demo accounts in one
would arrive in every test's database. Seed data belongs in a `@Profile("dev")`
`CommandLineRunner` — `DemoAccountSeeder` is the first one.

`FlywayOwnsTheSchemaTest` holds both halves: `migrationsCarryNoSeedData` reads the `.sql`
files, and `noStartupRunnerSeedsTheDatabaseOutsideTheDevProfile` asserts that a context
with no profile active has no `CommandLineRunner` or `ApplicationRunner` bean at all. The
second is by type rather than by name, so the next slice tempted to seed something is held
to the same profile guard.

## Writing the SQL

Hibernate's implicit naming strategy picks the names these files have to match:
`sourceAccountId` becomes `source_account_id`, and an embedded `Money` flattens into
`minor_units` / `currency` with no prefix. It will not split a one-letter word off the one
that follows it — `EntityWithoutAMigration` becomes `entity_withoutamigration`, not
`entity_without_a_migration`.

Column *types* are the sharper edge. `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` on Hibernate 7 and H2
maps to a **native H2 `enum (…)` column, not a `varchar`** — a migration writing
`varchar(3)` looks obviously right, matches every tutorial written before Hibernate 6.2,
and fails `validate` at startup. Pin the mapping with `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)` on
the component rather than writing an H2-specific type here; this schema still has to
survive the move to Postgres. `RecordAsEmbeddableSpikeTest` holds the evidence.

**Reserved words bite at `create table`, not at runtime.** `check` is one, so a
column of that name fails the migration outright — `V4__check_ledger.sql` calls its
column `required_check`, and the entity's field is named to produce that rather
than quoted into submission. A quoted identifier survives here and then has to be
repeated, quoted, in every hand-written query that touches it.

**Never write `in (…)` in a `check` constraint.** H2 compiles a constant `in` list into a
set ordered by *the session that parsed the DDL*, and evaluating the constraint later asks
that session for its comparison mode. Flyway's connection is closed by then, so every
insert into the table fails — valid rows included — with
`Check constraint invalid: "TRANSFERS_STATUS_IS_KNOWN: "`, which names the constraint and
reads exactly like a row that broke the rule. The migration applies, `validate` passes and
the application starts, so nothing goes wrong until the first write. An `or` chain of
equalities on one column folds into the same set and fails identically, and so does an
integer list.

Write `status = any (array['PENDING', 'SETTLED', 'REJECTED', 'EXPIRED'])` instead, as
`V2__transfers.sql` does: it survives the connection closing, reads almost exactly like
`in`, and is a shape Postgres takes too. A single `=`, a `between` and a column-to-column
comparison are all safe as well, which is why `V1__accounts.sql` never met this.

A nullable column takes `verdict is null or verdict = any (array[…])`, as
`V4__check_ledger.sql` does. The `or` there is with an `is null` and not with a second
equality, so it is not the chain that folds into a set — but the way to be sure of that is
a test that a bad value is *refused*, not one that a good row goes in.

Design decision 29 has the reasoning behind all of this, and the alternatives that were
rejected, for as long as those files are around; ticket 11's record has every constraint
shape that was measured.

```java
package hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.checks;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.EnumType;
import jakarta.persistence.Enumerated;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import org.hibernate.annotations.JdbcTypeCode;
import org.hibernate.type.SqlTypes;

import java.util.Objects;

/**
 * One Check a Transfer requires, and how that Check has answered it.
 *
 * <p>A Transfer's rows together are its Check Ledger, and they are written when the
 * Transfer is: the set of rows is fixed at request time, not a log that grows as parties
 * report things. The unique constraint on {@code (transfer_id, required_check)}
 * says the same in the table, and it is what will make a Check service's at-least-once
 * delivery safe to receive.
 *
 * <p><b>An unanswered Check has no Verdict, and the column is null.</b> The alternative —
 * a third {@code PENDING} constant on {@link Verdict}, which is the shape design decision
 * 8 sketched — would make "nobody has answered" one of the answers, and every reader would
 * then have to know which of the three is not really a Verdict. {@link
 * hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.TransferStatus} carries {@code PENDING} for the
 * opposite reason: a Transfer really is in that state. Nothing is in the state of having
 * given the null answer.
 *
 * <p><b>The Transfer is referenced by ID, not by association</b>, on {@code Transfer}'s own
 * precedent: a Transfer only ever leaves {@code PENDING} by a conditional update guarded on
 * the status it is leaving, and an association would offer a second way to reach one that
 * quietly skips that.
 *
 * <p><b>The identifier is surrogate rather than the pair that is unique</b>, on {@code
 * IdempotencyRecord}'s precedent: Spring Data decides between insert and merge from whether
 * the identifier is set, so an assigned key would turn every {@code save} into a
 * {@code SELECT} followed by an {@code UPDATE}. The uniqueness that matters is a named
 * constraint either way.
 *
 * <p>There is deliberately no mutator. Ticket 20 writes a Verdict as an update guarded on
 * the row still being unanswered, because two deliveries of the same Verdict have to leave
 * the Transfer advanced once; a setter would offer a second way to make that transition
 * that quietly is not atomic.
 */
@Entity
@Table(name = "check_ledger")
class CheckLedgerEntry {

	@Id
	@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
	private Long id;

	private Long transferId;

	// `check` is reserved in SQL, so the column this name produces is `required_check`.
	@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
	@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)
	private Check requiredCheck;

	// If left unannotated, JPA stores the verdict by ordinal. See design decision 29.
	@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
	@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)
	private Verdict verdict;

	protected CheckLedgerEntry() {
		// required by JPA
	}

	/**
	 * A row in any state it can hold, which is what {@link LedgerDecision#decide} is
	 * specified over and therefore has to be able to see.
	 *
	 * <p>Production never reaches this with a Verdict in hand — {@link #outstanding} is how
	 * a row comes into being, and the answer arrives later as an update. That is the
	 * distinction being drawn: constructing a row in a state is not the same operation as
	 * <em>transitioning</em> one into it, and only the transition has a race to lose.
	 */
	CheckLedgerEntry(Long transferId, Check requiredCheck, Verdict verdict) {
		this.transferId = Objects.requireNonNull(transferId, "a check is required of a transfer");
		this.requiredCheck = Objects.requireNonNull(requiredCheck, "a ledger row is one check");
		this.verdict = verdict;
	}

	/** Opens a Check on a Transfer with nobody having answered it yet. */
	static CheckLedgerEntry outstanding(Long transferId, Check requiredCheck) {
		return new CheckLedgerEntry(transferId, requiredCheck, null);
	}

	Long getId() {
		return id;
	}

	/**
	 * Whether this row is the one the given Check answers.
	 *
	 * <p>What it is for is telling the two causes of a guarded update matching nothing apart:
	 * the Check was already answered, or the Transfer never required it. Only the second is a
	 * caller naming something that does not exist.
	 */
	boolean isFor(Check check) {
		return requiredCheck == check;
	}

	/** Whether this Check has said no — the one answer that ends a Transfer on its own. */
	boolean isRejected() {
		return verdict == Verdict.REJECTED;
	}

	/** Whether anyone has answered this Check at all, either way. */
	boolean isAnswered() {
		return verdict != null;
	}
}
```

### `.../checks/CheckLedgerRepository.java` (full)

```java
package hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.checks;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Modifying;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.repository.Repository;

import java.util.List;

/**
 * Persistence for {@link CheckLedgerEntry}, package-private so that reaching it from
 * another slice does not compile (design decision 30).
 *
 * <p>The bare {@link Repository} marker rather than {@code JpaRepository}, on {@code
 * Account}'s precedent: it declares nothing, so every method here is one with a call site
 * today. The two ticket 20 brought — the read that a Verdict's decision is made over, and
 * the update guarded on the row still being unanswered — are below.
 */
interface CheckLedgerRepository extends Repository<CheckLedgerEntry, Long> {

	/** Opens one Check on one Transfer, which is how a ledger row comes to exist. */
	CheckLedgerEntry save(CheckLedgerEntry entry);

	/** One Transfer's whole Check Ledger, which is what {@link LedgerDecision#decide} reads. */
	List<CheckLedgerEntry> findAllByTransferId(Long transferId);

	/**
	 * Writes a Verdict into the one row that is still outstanding for that Check, and
	 * reports how many rows that was — one, or none because somebody has already answered.
	 *
	 * <p><b>{@code verdict is null} is the guard, and it is what makes a Check service's
	 * at-least-once delivery safe.</b> A second delivery of the same Verdict matches no row
	 * and writes nothing, so the ledger keeps the answer it already had; a contradicting one
	 * cannot overwrite it either. A read-then-write would be the same rule with a window in
	 * the middle where both deliveries see the row unanswered.
	 *
	 * <p>A bulk update rather than a mutator on the entity, on {@code IdempotencyRecord}'s
	 * precedent: a setter would offer a second way to make this transition that quietly is
	 * not atomic. {@link CheckLedgerEntry} therefore has none.
	 */
	@Modifying
	@Query("""
			UPDATE CheckLedgerEntry entry SET entry.verdict = :verdict
			WHERE entry.transferId = :transferId
			  AND entry.requiredCheck = :check
			  AND entry.verdict IS NULL
			""")
	int answer(Long transferId, Check check, Verdict verdict);
}
```

### Entity conventions distilled

- **Tabs for indentation** everywhere (Spring's own style). Blank line between every field.
- `@Entity` + `@Table(name = "…")` always explicit, even where the implicit name matches.
- `@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` on a `private Long id;` — **always a surrogate id**, never a natural/assigned key (Spring Data would then `merge` instead of `insert`).
- **Every enum field gets both** `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` **and** `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)`, with the inline comment `// If left unannotated, JPA stores the status by ordinal. See design decision 29.` The `@JdbcTypeCode` is mandatory or `validate` fails (H2 native `enum` column).
- Timestamps are `java.time.Instant`, **passed in as a constructor parameter**, never `Instant.now()` (the `Clock` bean on `GlobalPaymentServiceApplication` is the one source of now). Field name `createdAt` → column `created_at`.
- `protected NoArgs() { // required by JPA }` — exactly that comment.
- All constructor args guarded by `Objects.requireNonNull(x, "a lowercase domain sentence")`.
- **No setters, ever.** Every state transition is a `@Modifying @Query` guarded update on the repository, with the "a setter would offer a second way … that quietly is not atomic" justification.
- Entity class is **package-private** (`class CheckLedgerEntry`, `class IdempotencyRecord`) unless another slice must name it (`public class Transfer`).
- Repositories extend the **bare `org.springframework.data.repository.Repository`**, never `JpaRepository`/`CrudRepository` — "it declares nothing, so every method here is one with a call site today". Package-private interface. Text blocks for JPQL, uppercase JPQL keywords, `entry`/`transfer` as the alias (not `e`/`t`).
- Javadoc is long, argumentative prose: `<p>` paragraphs, `<b>`/`<em>` for the claim sentence, references to `design decision N`, `ticket N`, and named test classes.

## 4. The other two "public ports" — **neither is built yet**

This is the most important correction to your assumptions. The three ports are named in `docs/design-decisions/00-initial-decisions.md` §30:

```
├── idempotency/   IdempotentExecution (public) · JDBC impl package-private
├── fx/            ExchangeRateProvider (public) · HTTP client package-private
├── outbox/        EventPublisher (public) · OutboxPoller package-private
```
> "The three public ports are exactly §3, §11/§12 and the FX client"

**None of the three types exists on disk.** `fx/` contains only `CurrencyConversion.java`, `ConversionResult.java`, `package-info.java` — the port arrives with ticket 25. `idempotency/` contains no public type at all; its `package-info.java` says so explicitly:

> "The port design decision 3 describes … is not here yet. It arrives with the first caller that has a use for it, which is the duplicate resolution of ticket 17."

Likewise §30's ticket-16 amendment: *"the slice ships the storage under the port and not the port itself … Nothing in the package is public, so the line's `IdempotentExecution (public)` is what ticket 17 makes true."*

**So `EventPublisher` will be the first of the three ports actually written.** The shapes to copy from instead:

### a) The public-facade-over-package-private-internals shape — `transfers/checks/CheckLedger.java`

The single closest precedent. `@Component`, **public class with public methods** (because `@Transactional` on non-public is silently ignored), package-private constructor, package-private collaborators:

```java
@Component
public class CheckLedger {

	private final CheckPolicy policy;

	private final CheckLedgerRepository entries;

	CheckLedger(CheckPolicy policy, CheckLedgerRepository entries) {
		this.policy = policy;
		this.entries = entries;
	}

	@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
	public void openFor(Transfer transfer) { … }
```

with the visibility rationale stated in its Javadoc:

> "The method is public on a package-private-by-default design because `@Transactional` on a non-public method is silently ignored under proxy-based AOP — the trap `hu.bankmonitor.payments` documents. The class is public for the ordinary reason: `FundsReservation` is in the parent package and has to name it."

Same shape at `accounts/AccountLocking.java` (`@Component public class AccountLocking`, package-private ctor, `@Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY) public LockedAccounts lockForTransfer(...)`).

Note: this codebase uses `@Component` for these facades and `@Service` for the transaction-owning application services (`FundsReservation`, `VerdictRecording`, `IdempotencyClaims` — all `@Service` + package-private class + public `@Transactional` methods). There is **no `@Configuration` bean-method style** except `mockfx/MockExchangeRateProvider` (`@Configuration @Profile(...)` holding a `WebSecurityCustomizer` bean) and the `Clock` bean on the application class.

### b) The interface-with-one-method shape — sealed/enum vocabulary

`fx/ConversionResult.java` is the precedent for a small public interface with Javadoc that says why the shape is what it is; `Check`/`Verdict` are the precedent for public enums that are part of the schema:

> *(Check.java)* "The constants are stored by name, so they are part of the schema: `V4__check_ledger.sql` lists them in a check constraint, and renaming one is a migration rather than a refactor."

### c) `mockfx/FlakinessSettings.java` — the config-properties shape, if the poller gets a configurable interval

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(FlakinessSettings.PREFIX)
@Validated
record FlakinessSettings(
		@DecimalMin("0.0") @DecimalMax("1.0") @DefaultValue("0.3") double failureRate,
		@DefaultValue("200ms") Duration latency) {

	static final String PREFIX = "payments.mock-fx";
}
```
Registered via `@EnableConfigurationProperties(FlakinessSettings.class)` on the slice's `@Configuration`. Defaults live in the record ("so there is one copy of them, and so that the settings cannot be half-absent"), namespace prefix is `payments.<slice>`.

### 5a. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/ModuleBoundariesHoldTest.java` (full, shown above in tool output; the load-bearing parts)

			.that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Controller")
			.or().areMetaAnnotatedWith(Controller.class)
			.should().dependOnClassesThat().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Repository")
			.orShould().dependOnClassesThat().areAssignableTo(Repository.class)
			.because("a controller holding a repository has skipped the service that owns the transaction")
			.allowEmptyShould(true);

Three tests: `everyPackageOfTheDesignExists` (asserts `outbox` is on the classpath — the existing `package-info.java` is what puts it there), `theSlicesAreFreeOfCycles`, `noControllerReachesARepository`. Plus a `@Nested class RulesFailWhenViolated` that runs each rule against deliberate fixtures under `hu.bankmonitor.testsupport.boundaryviolations.*` and asserts the rule *fails*. **Convention: every new prohibition rule ships with a falsification fixture.**

**Implications for ticket 27:**
- `slices().matching("hu.bankmonitor.payments.(*)..")` — `outbox` must not depend on `transfers` (ticket 28 has `transfers` writing outbox rows; the dependency runs one way). Do not import anything from `transfers` into `outbox`.
- No class named `*Controller` or meta-annotated `@Controller` may depend on anything named `*Repository` or assignable to `Repository`. The poller is not a controller, so it's fine.

### 5b. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/transfers/NothingButTheReservationCreatesATransferTest.java` — **the "which classes may write entities" rule**

```java
	private static final ArchRule ONLY_THE_RESERVATION_WRITES_A_TRANSFER = noClasses()
			.that().doNotHaveFullyQualifiedName(FundsReservation.class.getName())
			.should().dependOnClassesThat().haveFullyQualifiedName(TransferRepository.class.getName())
			.because("a Transfer written anywhere else would be PENDING against an empty check ledger");
```

The rule is by **dependency on the interface**, not by call. Its Javadoc names the axis explicitly:

> "So the axis is not read against write … It is restricted against unrestricted. Creating a Transfer is restricted because one written anywhere else would be `PENDING` against an empty Check Ledger; advancing one is not, because the guard travels with the statement."

There is **no analogous rule for outbox rows yet**. If you add one, the established pattern is: a separate `Repository` interface per access kind (`TransferRepository` = write only, `TransferQueries` = reads, `TransferTransitions` = lock + guarded update), each package-private, so that "a reader cannot call `save` because it cannot name it".

### 5c. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/LockedPathTouchesOnlyTheDatabaseTest.java` — the reachability walk

```java
	private static final DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE = resideInAnyPackage(
			"java.net..",
			"java.io..",
			"java.nio.file..",
			"jakarta.servlet..",
			"org.springframework.web..",
			"org.springframework.http..",

**This is the rule ticket 27 can break.** `FundsReservation` and `VerdictRecording` are lock holders; the walk is transitive over application classes. When ticket 28 makes them write outbox events, anything reachable from `EventPublisher` must not touch `java.net`, `java.io`, `org.springframework.web/http`, or the `fx`/`mockfx` packages. A log-line `EventPublisher` is fine; note that the walk stops at interfaces, so a port declared in `outbox` with an impl in `outbox` is walked (both are application classes) — keep the log implementation free of `java.io` (SLF4J is `org.slf4j`, not matched).

`hu.bankmonitor.payments.outbox..` is **not** currently in `IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE`, which is consistent with the outbox being a database write held inside the lock.

## 7. Logging conventions

Only **three** log statements exist in `src/main/java`. There is **no structured/key-value logging library** — no logstash-encoder, no `StructuredArguments`, no `atInfo().addKeyValue()`, no MDC. `grep` for all of those returns nothing. So "a structured log line" means SLF4J parameterised placeholders, not fluent key-value.

The house style:

**Declaration** (always `private static final Logger log`, lowercase `log`, `LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class)`, placed *after* other `static final` constants and *before* instance fields):

```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/DemoAccountSeeder.java:43
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(DemoAccountSeeder.class);
```
```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/mockfx/MockExchangeRateController.java:50
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MockExchangeRateController.class);
```

**Example 1 — info with `{}` placeholders** (`DemoAccountSeeder.java:62`):

```java
	@Override
	public void run(String... args) {
		List<Account> seeded = accounts.saveAll(OPENING_BALANCES.stream().map(Account::new).toList());

		log.info("Seeded {} demo accounts for the '{}' profile", seeded.size(), DEV_PROFILE);
	}
```

**Example 2 — error with the throwable as last arg** (`MockExchangeRateController.java:108`), and note the Javadoc explains *why the line exists*:

```java
	/**
	 * …
	 * <p>It is logged before it is swallowed. The response deliberately says nothing about
	 * what went wrong — a third party's would not — so without this line the one place the
	 * defect could be seen is the place that discards it.
	 */
	@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
	ResponseEntity<ProviderFault> anythingElse(Exception failure) {
		log.error("The stand-in FX provider failed to answer a request", failure);
		return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
				.body(new ProviderFault("rate_service_error", "The rate service failed to answer."));
	}
```

**Example 3 — the one place a different name is used** (`src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/ProblemDocumentAdvice.java:194`), inherited `logger` from `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`, string concatenation:

```java
		logger.error("Unhandled exception, answered as " + ProblemType.INTERNAL_ERROR.urn(), exception);
```

Message style: **sentence case, capital first letter, no trailing period, no prefixes/brackets/tags.** Values interpolated via `{}` (quoted with `'…'` when a string identifier). No log levels below `info` are used anywhere.

	@Test
	@DisplayName("a claim is committed before the caller returns, and another connection sees it")
	void aClaimIsCommittedBeforeTheCallerReturns() throws SQLException {
		try (Connection onlooker = dataSource.getConnection()) {
			claims.claim(KEY, PAYLOAD_HASH);

			assertThat(readStatusThrough(onlooker)).isEqualTo("IN_PROGRESS");
		}

		assertThat(storedPayloadHash()).isEqualTo(PAYLOAD_HASH);
		assertThat(storedResponseBody()).isNull();
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("a second claim of a live key is refused by the constraint, not merged over it")
	void aSecondClaimOfALiveKeyIsRefusedByTheConstraint() {
		claims.claim(KEY, PAYLOAD_HASH);

		assertThatThrownBy(() -> claims.claim(KEY, A_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD_HASH))
				.isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
				.hasStackTraceContaining("IDEMPOTENCY_RECORDS_KEY_IS_UNIQUE");

		assertThat(storedPayloadHash()).isEqualTo(PAYLOAD_HASH);
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("the table refuses a status the domain has no name for")
	void refusesAStatusTheDomainHasNoNameFor() {
		assertThatThrownBy(() -> insertRecord("ABANDONED", null))
				.hasStackTraceContaining("IDEMPOTENCY_RECORDS_STATUS_IS_KNOWN");
	}

### Representative `@SpringBootTest` integration test — base class + scenario base + a test

`src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/testsupport/BootedApplicationTest.java` (full):

```java
package hu.bankmonitor.testsupport;

import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.server.LocalServerPort;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.client.RestTestClient;

/**
 * Base for tests that need the whole application running on a real port.
 *
 * <p>The configuration lives here rather than being repeated on each subclass for a
 * reason beyond tidiness: Spring caches one application context per distinct
 * configuration, so two classes differing by a single annotation pay two boots. Holding
 * the annotations in one place makes the shared context structural rather than a
 * coincidence the next edit could break.
 *
 * <p>{@code RANDOM_PORT} rather than MockMvc, because the claims these tests make are
 * about the servlet container itself — that a request reaches a listening socket, and
 * what kind of thread Tomcat serves it on. MockMvc would bypass it and prove neither.
 */
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(ThreadProbeController.class)
public abstract class BootedApplicationTest {

	@LocalServerPort
	private int port;

	/**
	 * A client bound to the running server. {@code TestRestTemplate} is gone in Spring
	 * Boot 4; {@code RestTestClient} is its Spring Framework 7 replacement.
	 */
	protected RestTestClient client() {
		return RestTestClient.bindToServer().baseUrl("http://localhost:" + port).build();
	}
}
```

Its Javadoc states the two rules that will bite the outbox tests:

> "**Nothing here is transactional, and that is the point.** A `@Transactional` test method makes every write it performs invisible to any other connection and rolls the lot back at the end … Every subclass needs real commits, so the price is paying for the cleanup by hand."
> "The tables are emptied before each method as well as after: one in-memory H2 database is shared by every test in the suite, whichever application context booted it."
> "Rows go in and come back out in SQL rather than through the entities, so what is asserted is what reached the database — a round trip through the mapping under test would agree with itself whatever it wrote."

And the concrete test, `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/transfers/EveryTransferOpensItsCheckLedgerTest.java`:

```java
class EveryTransferOpensItsCheckLedgerTest extends TransferScenario {

	private static final long SOURCE = 1L;
	private static final long DESTINATION = 2L;
	private static final long OPENING_BALANCE = 250_00L;

	@Autowired
	private CheckLedger ledger;

	@BeforeEach
	void openBothAccounts() {
		openAccount(SOURCE, OPENING_BALANCE, EUR);
		openAccount(DESTINATION, 0L, EUR);
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("requesting a Transfer opens one outstanding row per required Check")
	void opensOneOutstandingRowPerRequiredCheck() {
		Transfer requested = reservation.reserve(transferOf(80_00L, SOURCE, DESTINATION));

		assertThat(checkLedgerRows())
				.allSatisfy(row -> {
					assertThat(row).containsEntry("TRANSFER_ID", requested.getId());
					assertThat(row).containsEntry("VERDICT", null);
				})
				.extracting(row -> row.get("REQUIRED_CHECK"))
				.containsExactlyInAnyOrder("FRAUD", "MANUAL_APPROVAL");
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("a refused Transfer leaves no ledger behind either")
	void writesNoLedgerWhenTheTransferIsRefused() {
		assertThatThrownBy(() -> reservation.reserve(transferOf(OPENING_BALANCE + 1, SOURCE, DESTINATION)))
				.isInstanceOf(InsufficientFundsException.class);

		assertThat(transferRows()).isEmpty();
		assertThat(checkLedgerRows()).isEmpty();
	}
```

**This last one is the exact template for ticket 27's "an event written in a transaction that rolls back is never published".** Note the H2 column keys come back **UPPERCASE** (`"TRANSFER_ID"`, `"VERDICT"`).

### Fakes over mocks

There is no Mockito usage in any test read. Where a collaborator must be faked, a hand-written static nested `private static final class` implementing the package-private repository is used, e.g. `FakeLedgerRows implements CheckLedgerRepository` in `RecordingAVerdictAnswersOneOutstandingCheckTest`, with unsupported methods throwing `AssertionError`:

```java
		@Override
		public CheckLedgerEntry save(CheckLedgerEntry entry) {
			throw new AssertionError("recording a Verdict opens no rows");
		}
```

### Assertions

AssertJ throughout — static imports of `assertThat`, `assertThatThrownBy`, `assertThatCode` from `org.assertj.core.api.Assertions`. JUnit 5 (`@Test`, `@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`). No Hamcrest, no JUnit assertions.

### `src/test/resources/`

Contains **only** `src/test/resources/db/testmigration/moneymapping/V1__money_embedding_host.sql`. There is **no test `application.properties`, no test profile file, no logback-test.xml.** Test-specific properties go inline via `@TestPropertySource(properties = "…")` on the test class (see the `@DataJpaTest` above) — deliberate, because each distinct configuration costs another cached application context (design decision 25).

### `V4__check_ledger.sql` (full)

```sql
create table check_ledger (
    id             bigint generated by default as identity primary key,

    transfer_id    bigint      not null,

    -- `check` is reserved in SQL, so the entity's field is `requiredCheck`. See 19-check-ledger-and-policy.md.
    required_check varchar(15) not null,

    -- Nullable on purpose: no Verdict is how the table says this Check has not answered yet.
    verdict        varchar(8),

    constraint check_ledger_transfer
        foreign key (transfer_id) references transfers (id),

    -- The ledger is fixed when the Transfer is written, not a log of what was reported.
    constraint check_ledger_one_row_per_check
        unique (transfer_id, required_check),

    -- `= any (array[…])`, never `in (…)` — the README beside this file has why.
    constraint check_ledger_check_is_known
        check (required_check = any (array['FRAUD', 'MANUAL_APPROVAL'])),
    constraint check_ledger_verdict_is_known
        check (verdict is null or verdict = any (array['APPROVED', 'REJECTED']))
);
```

### `V2__transfers.sql` (full)

```sql
create table transfers (
    id                          bigint generated by default as identity primary key,

    source_account_id           bigint      not null,
    destination_account_id      bigint      not null,

    -- Four columns for two Money embeddables, named by Transfer's @AttributeOverrides.
    debited_amount_minor_units  bigint      not null,
    debited_amount_currency     varchar(3)  not null,
    credited_amount_minor_units bigint      not null,
    credited_amount_currency    varchar(3)  not null,

    status                      varchar(8)  not null,

    created_at                  timestamp(6) with time zone not null,

    constraint transfers_source_account
        foreign key (source_account_id) references accounts (id),
    constraint transfers_destination_account
        foreign key (destination_account_id) references accounts (id),

    -- All three hold for rows the entity cannot write. See 11-transfer-entity.md.
    -- `= any (array[…])`, never `in (…)` — the README beside this file has why.
    constraint transfers_status_is_known
        check (status = any (array['PENDING', 'SETTLED', 'REJECTED', 'EXPIRED'])),
    constraint transfers_two_distinct_accounts
        check (source_account_id <> destination_account_id),
    constraint transfers_positive_amounts
        check (debited_amount_minor_units > 0 and credited_amount_minor_units > 0)
);
```

### Extracted dialect/style rules

- **All lowercase SQL keywords.** Column names left-aligned, types aligned in a column, blank lines grouping related columns.
- **Id:** `id bigint generated by default as identity primary key` — verbatim in all four migrations. `generated by default` (not `always`) is load-bearing: tests insert explicit ids (`TransferScenario.openAccount`).
- **Timestamp:** `timestamp(6) with time zone not null` (only occurrence, `transfers.created_at`, maps to `java.time.Instant`).
- **Enum-backed columns:** `varchar(N)` where N is the longest constant, plus a named `check … = any (array[…])`. `varchar(15)` for `MANUAL_APPROVAL`, `varchar(8)` for `REJECTED`/`APPROVED`, `varchar(11)` for `IN_PROGRESS`.
- **Constraint naming:** `<table>_<what_it_says>`, snake_case, no `chk_`/`fk_` prefixes — `transfers_status_is_known`, `check_ledger_one_row_per_check`, `idempotency_records_response_only_when_succeeded`, `check_ledger_transfer` (FK).
- **`in (…)` is forbidden in check constraints** — H2 folds it into a session-ordered set and every later insert fails. Always `col = any (array[…])`; nullable columns take `col is null or col = any (array[…])`.
- **Comments:** `--` lines *above* the thing, stating the non-obvious *why*, often ending with a pointer to `NN-<ticket>.md`. No comment restates a column name.
- **No index exists anywhere in the codebase yet.** `grep -i index src/main/resources/db/migration src/main/java` returns only an unrelated `step.getIndex()`. Ticket 27's unsent index will be the first, so there is no index naming precedent — but §29 anticipates it:

> *(00-initial-decisions.md ~line 1029)* "the natural home for the indexes the design implies: the outbox poller's `WHERE sent_at IS NULL`, the reaper's `WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND deadline < ?`."

The constraint convention (`<table>_<what>`) is the only naming precedent to extend, e.g. `outbox_events_unsent`.

### `db/migration/README.md` (full)

```markdown
# Migrations

Flyway owns this schema. `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` is on, so Hibernate
checks the entities against whatever these files produced and never generates DDL itself.
A mismatch is a startup failure naming the table or column it could not find.

## One migration per slice

Each ticket that introduces a table or a column ships the migration for it, in the same
commit as the entity: `V1__accounts.sql`, `V2__transfers.sql`, and so on, including the
later ones that only add a column. Do not write ahead of the entities — a migration for a
table nothing maps yet is the one artefact `validate` cannot check while you are writing
it.

Numbers are global and never reused. Applied migrations are immutable: to change
something a released migration created, add the next `V`.

## Invariants belong here too

`V1__accounts.sql` carries named `check` constraints, and they are not a substitute for
the domain check above them — an overdraft has to be refused in the service, under the
lock, to reach the caller as a `422` rather than a constraint violation. What the
constraint adds is that a path *around* that check fails the write. Name them, so a
violation says which rule was broken.

Hand-written constraints are fine under `validate`. The trouble design decision 29 records
is with Hibernate's *schema export* emitting one under `create-drop`, which is a setting
this application never uses.

## Seed data does not go here

A migration runs everywhere Flyway runs, the test suite included, so demo accounts in one
would arrive in every test's database. Seed data belongs in a `@Profile("dev")`
`CommandLineRunner` — `DemoAccountSeeder` is the first one.

`FlywayOwnsTheSchemaTest` holds both halves: `migrationsCarryNoSeedData` reads the `.sql`
files, and `noStartupRunnerSeedsTheDatabaseOutsideTheDevProfile` asserts that a context
with no profile active has no `CommandLineRunner` or `ApplicationRunner` bean at all. The
second is by type rather than by name, so the next slice tempted to seed something is held
to the same profile guard.

## Writing the SQL

Hibernate's implicit naming strategy picks the names these files have to match:
`sourceAccountId` becomes `source_account_id`, and an embedded `Money` flattens into
`minor_units` / `currency` with no prefix. It will not split a one-letter word off the one
that follows it — `EntityWithoutAMigration` becomes `entity_withoutamigration`, not
`entity_without_a_migration`.

Column *types* are the sharper edge. `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` on Hibernate 7 and H2
maps to a **native H2 `enum (…)` column, not a `varchar`** — a migration writing
`varchar(3)` looks obviously right, matches every tutorial written before Hibernate 6.2,
and fails `validate` at startup. Pin the mapping with `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)` on
the component rather than writing an H2-specific type here; this schema still has to
survive the move to Postgres. `RecordAsEmbeddableSpikeTest` holds the evidence.

**Reserved words bite at `create table`, not at runtime.** `check` is one, so a
column of that name fails the migration outright — `V4__check_ledger.sql` calls its
column `required_check`, and the entity's field is named to produce that rather
than quoted into submission. A quoted identifier survives here and then has to be
repeated, quoted, in every hand-written query that touches it.

**Never write `in (…)` in a `check` constraint.** H2 compiles a constant `in` list into a
set ordered by *the session that parsed the DDL*, and evaluating the constraint later asks
that session for its comparison mode. Flyway's connection is closed by then, so every
insert into the table fails — valid rows included — with
`Check constraint invalid: "TRANSFERS_STATUS_IS_KNOWN: "`, which names the constraint and
reads exactly like a row that broke the rule. The migration applies, `validate` passes and
the application starts, so nothing goes wrong until the first write. An `or` chain of
equalities on one column folds into the same set and fails identically, and so does an
integer list.

Write `status = any (array['PENDING', 'SETTLED', 'REJECTED', 'EXPIRED'])` instead, as
`V2__transfers.sql` does: it survives the connection closing, reads almost exactly like
`in`, and is a shape Postgres takes too. A single `=`, a `between` and a column-to-column
comparison are all safe as well, which is why `V1__accounts.sql` never met this.

A nullable column takes `verdict is null or verdict = any (array[…])`, as
`V4__check_ledger.sql` does. The `or` there is with an `is null` and not with a second
equality, so it is not the chain that folds into a set — but the way to be sure of that is
a test that a bad value is *refused*, not one that a good row goes in.

Design decision 29 has the reasoning behind all of this, and the alternatives that were
rejected, for as long as those files are around; ticket 11's record has every constraint
shape that was measured.

package hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.checks;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.EnumType;
import jakarta.persistence.Enumerated;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import org.hibernate.annotations.JdbcTypeCode;
import org.hibernate.type.SqlTypes;

import java.util.Objects;

/**
 * One Check a Transfer requires, and how that Check has answered it.
 *
 * <p>A Transfer's rows together are its Check Ledger, and they are written when the
 * Transfer is: the set of rows is fixed at request time, not a log that grows as parties
 * report things. The unique constraint on {@code (transfer_id, required_check)}
 * says the same in the table, and it is what will make a Check service's at-least-once
 * delivery safe to receive.
 *
 * <p><b>An unanswered Check has no Verdict, and the column is null.</b> The alternative —
 * a third {@code PENDING} constant on {@link Verdict}, which is the shape design decision
 * 8 sketched — would make "nobody has answered" one of the answers, and every reader would
 * then have to know which of the three is not really a Verdict. {@link
 * hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.TransferStatus} carries {@code PENDING} for the
 * opposite reason: a Transfer really is in that state. Nothing is in the state of having
 * given the null answer.
 *
 * <p><b>The Transfer is referenced by ID, not by association</b>, on {@code Transfer}'s own
 * precedent: a Transfer only ever leaves {@code PENDING} by a conditional update guarded on
 * the status it is leaving, and an association would offer a second way to reach one that
 * quietly skips that.
 *
 * <p><b>The identifier is surrogate rather than the pair that is unique</b>, on {@code
 * IdempotencyRecord}'s precedent: Spring Data decides between insert and merge from whether
 * the identifier is set, so an assigned key would turn every {@code save} into a
 * {@code SELECT} followed by an {@code UPDATE}. The uniqueness that matters is a named
 * constraint either way.
 *
 * <p>There is deliberately no mutator. Ticket 20 writes a Verdict as an update guarded on
 * the row still being unanswered, because two deliveries of the same Verdict have to leave
 * the Transfer advanced once; a setter would offer a second way to make that transition
 * that quietly is not atomic.
 */
@Entity
@Table(name = "check_ledger")
class CheckLedgerEntry {

	@Id
	@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
	private Long id;

	private Long transferId;

	// `check` is reserved in SQL, so the column this name produces is `required_check`.
	@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
	@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)
	private Check requiredCheck;

	// If left unannotated, JPA stores the verdict by ordinal. See design decision 29.
	@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
	@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)
	private Verdict verdict;

	protected CheckLedgerEntry() {
		// required by JPA
	}

	/**
	 * A row in any state it can hold, which is what {@link LedgerDecision#decide} is
	 * specified over and therefore has to be able to see.
	 *
	 * <p>Production never reaches this with a Verdict in hand — {@link #outstanding} is how
	 * a row comes into being, and the answer arrives later as an update. That is the
	 * distinction being drawn: constructing a row in a state is not the same operation as
	 * <em>transitioning</em> one into it, and only the transition has a race to lose.
	 */
	CheckLedgerEntry(Long transferId, Check requiredCheck, Verdict verdict) {
		this.transferId = Objects.requireNonNull(transferId, "a check is required of a transfer");
		this.requiredCheck = Objects.requireNonNull(requiredCheck, "a ledger row is one check");
		this.verdict = verdict;
	}

	/** Opens a Check on a Transfer with nobody having answered it yet. */
	static CheckLedgerEntry outstanding(Long transferId, Check requiredCheck) {
		return new CheckLedgerEntry(transferId, requiredCheck, null);
	}

	Long getId() {
		return id;
	}

	/**
	 * Whether this row is the one the given Check answers.
	 *
	 * <p>What it is for is telling the two causes of a guarded update matching nothing apart:
	 * the Check was already answered, or the Transfer never required it. Only the second is a
	 * caller naming something that does not exist.
	 */
	boolean isFor(Check check) {
		return requiredCheck == check;
	}

	/** Whether this Check has said no — the one answer that ends a Transfer on its own. */
	boolean isRejected() {
		return verdict == Verdict.REJECTED;
	}

	/** Whether anyone has answered this Check at all, either way. */
	boolean isAnswered() {
		return verdict != null;
	}
}
```

### `.../checks/CheckLedgerRepository.java` (full)

```java
package hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.checks;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Modifying;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.repository.Repository;

import java.util.List;

/**
 * Persistence for {@link CheckLedgerEntry}, package-private so that reaching it from
 * another slice does not compile (design decision 30).
 *
 * <p>The bare {@link Repository} marker rather than {@code JpaRepository}, on {@code
 * Account}'s precedent: it declares nothing, so every method here is one with a call site
 * today. The two ticket 20 brought — the read that a Verdict's decision is made over, and
 * the update guarded on the row still being unanswered — are below.
 */
interface CheckLedgerRepository extends Repository<CheckLedgerEntry, Long> {

	/** Opens one Check on one Transfer, which is how a ledger row comes to exist. */
	CheckLedgerEntry save(CheckLedgerEntry entry);

	/** One Transfer's whole Check Ledger, which is what {@link LedgerDecision#decide} reads. */
	List<CheckLedgerEntry> findAllByTransferId(Long transferId);

	/**
	 * Writes a Verdict into the one row that is still outstanding for that Check, and
	 * reports how many rows that was — one, or none because somebody has already answered.
	 *
	 * <p><b>{@code verdict is null} is the guard, and it is what makes a Check service's
	 * at-least-once delivery safe.</b> A second delivery of the same Verdict matches no row
	 * and writes nothing, so the ledger keeps the answer it already had; a contradicting one
	 * cannot overwrite it either. A read-then-write would be the same rule with a window in
	 * the middle where both deliveries see the row unanswered.
	 *
	 * <p>A bulk update rather than a mutator on the entity, on {@code IdempotencyRecord}'s
	 * precedent: a setter would offer a second way to make this transition that quietly is
	 * not atomic. {@link CheckLedgerEntry} therefore has none.
	 */
	@Modifying
	@Query("""
			UPDATE CheckLedgerEntry entry SET entry.verdict = :verdict
			WHERE entry.transferId = :transferId
			  AND entry.requiredCheck = :check
			  AND entry.verdict IS NULL
			""")
	int answer(Long transferId, Check check, Verdict verdict);
}
```

### Entity conventions distilled

- **Tabs for indentation** everywhere (Spring's own style). Blank line between every field.
- `@Entity` + `@Table(name = "…")` always explicit, even where the implicit name matches.
- `@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` on a `private Long id;` — **always a surrogate id**, never a natural/assigned key (Spring Data would then `merge` instead of `insert`).
- **Every enum field gets both** `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` **and** `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)`, with the inline comment `// If left unannotated, JPA stores the status by ordinal. See design decision 29.` The `@JdbcTypeCode` is mandatory or `validate` fails (H2 native `enum` column).
- Timestamps are `java.time.Instant`, **passed in as a constructor parameter**, never `Instant.now()` (the `Clock` bean on `GlobalPaymentServiceApplication` is the one source of now). Field name `createdAt` → column `created_at`.
- `protected NoArgs() { // required by JPA }` — exactly that comment.
- All constructor args guarded by `Objects.requireNonNull(x, "a lowercase domain sentence")`.
- **No setters, ever.** Every state transition is a `@Modifying @Query` guarded update on the repository, with the "a setter would offer a second way … that quietly is not atomic" justification.
- Entity class is **package-private** (`class CheckLedgerEntry`, `class IdempotencyRecord`) unless another slice must name it (`public class Transfer`).
- Repositories extend the **bare `org.springframework.data.repository.Repository`**, never `JpaRepository`/`CrudRepository` — "it declares nothing, so every method here is one with a call site today". Package-private interface. Text blocks for JPQL, uppercase JPQL keywords, `entry`/`transfer` as the alias (not `e`/`t`).
- Javadoc is long, argumentative prose: `<p>` paragraphs, `<b>`/`<em>` for the claim sentence, references to `design decision N`, `ticket N`, and named test classes.

## 4. The other two "public ports" — **neither is built yet**

This is the most important correction to your assumptions. The three ports are named in `docs/design-decisions/00-initial-decisions.md` §30:

```
├── idempotency/   IdempotentExecution (public) · JDBC impl package-private
├── fx/            ExchangeRateProvider (public) · HTTP client package-private
├── outbox/        EventPublisher (public) · OutboxPoller package-private
```
> "The three public ports are exactly §3, §11/§12 and the FX client"

**None of the three types exists on disk.** `fx/` contains only `CurrencyConversion.java`, `ConversionResult.java`, `package-info.java` — the port arrives with ticket 25. `idempotency/` contains no public type at all; its `package-info.java` says so explicitly:

> "The port design decision 3 describes … is not here yet. It arrives with the first caller that has a use for it, which is the duplicate resolution of ticket 17."

Likewise §30's ticket-16 amendment: *"the slice ships the storage under the port and not the port itself … Nothing in the package is public, so the line's `IdempotentExecution (public)` is what ticket 17 makes true."*

**So `EventPublisher` will be the first of the three ports actually written.** The shapes to copy from instead:

### a) The public-facade-over-package-private-internals shape — `transfers/checks/CheckLedger.java`

The single closest precedent. `@Component`, **public class with public methods** (because `@Transactional` on non-public is silently ignored), package-private constructor, package-private collaborators:

```java

```

with the visibility rationale stated in its Javadoc:

> "The method is public on a package-private-by-default design because `@Transactional` on a non-public method is silently ignored under proxy-based AOP — the trap `hu.bankmonitor.payments` documents. The class is public for the ordinary reason: `FundsReservation` is in the parent package and has to name it."

Same shape at `accounts/AccountLocking.java` (`@Component public class AccountLocking`, package-private ctor, `@Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY) public LockedAccounts lockForTransfer(...)`).

Note: this codebase uses `@Component` for these facades and `@Service` for the transaction-owning application services (`FundsReservation`, `VerdictRecording`, `IdempotencyClaims` — all `@Service` + package-private class + public `@Transactional` methods). There is **no `@Configuration` bean-method style** except `mockfx/MockExchangeRateProvider` (`@Configuration @Profile(...)` holding a `WebSecurityCustomizer` bean) and the `Clock` bean on the application class.

### b) The interface-with-one-method shape — sealed/enum vocabulary

`fx/ConversionResult.java` is the precedent for a small public interface with Javadoc that says why the shape is what it is; `Check`/`Verdict` are the precedent for public enums that are part of the schema:

> *(Check.java)* "The constants are stored by name, so they are part of the schema: `V4__check_ledger.sql` lists them in a check constraint, and renaming one is a migration rather than a refactor."

			.because("a Transfer written anywhere else would be PENDING against an empty check ledger");
```

The rule is by **dependency on the interface**, not by call. Its Javadoc names the axis explicitly:

> "So the axis is not read against write … It is restricted against unrestricted. Creating a Transfer is restricted because one written anywhere else would be `PENDING` against an empty Check Ledger; advancing one is not, because the guard travels with the statement."

There is **no analogous rule for outbox rows yet**. If you add one, the established pattern is: a separate `Repository` interface per access kind (`TransferRepository` = write only, `TransferQueries` = reads, `TransferTransitions` = lock + guarded update), each package-private, so that "a reader cannot call `save` because it cannot name it".

### 5c. `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/LockedPathTouchesOnlyTheDatabaseTest.java` — the reachability walk

```java
	private static final DescribedPredicate<JavaClass> IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE = resideInAnyPackage(
			"java.net..",
			"java.io..",
			"java.nio.file..",
			"jakarta.servlet..",
			"org.springframework.web..",
			"org.springframework.http..",
			"hu.bankmonitor.payments.fx..",
			"hu.bankmonitor.payments.mockfx..");

	private static final List<String> LOCK_HOLDERS = List.of(
			AccountLocking.class.getName(),
			"hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.FundsReservation",
			"hu.bankmonitor.payments.transfers.VerdictRecording");
```

**This is the rule ticket 27 can break.** `FundsReservation` and `VerdictRecording` are lock holders; the walk is transitive over application classes. When ticket 28 makes them write outbox events, anything reachable from `EventPublisher` must not touch `java.net`, `java.io`, `org.springframework.web/http`, or the `fx`/`mockfx` packages. A log-line `EventPublisher` is fine; note that the walk stops at interfaces, so a port declared in `outbox` with an impl in `outbox` is walked (both are application classes) — keep the log implementation free of `java.io` (SLF4J is `org.slf4j`, not matched).

`hu.bankmonitor.payments.outbox..` is **not** currently in `IO_BEYOND_THE_DATABASE`, which is consistent with the outbox being a database write held inside the lock.

## 7. Logging conventions

Only **three** log statements exist in `src/main/java`. There is **no structured/key-value logging library** — no logstash-encoder, no `StructuredArguments`, no `atInfo().addKeyValue()`, no MDC. `grep` for all of those returns nothing. So "a structured log line" means SLF4J parameterised placeholders, not fluent key-value.

The house style:

**Declaration** (always `private static final Logger log`, lowercase `log`, `LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class)`, placed *after* other `static final` constants and *before* instance fields):

```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/accounts/DemoAccountSeeder.java:43
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(DemoAccountSeeder.class);
```
```java
// src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/mockfx/MockExchangeRateController.java:50
	private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MockExchangeRateController.class);
```

**Example 1 — info with `{}` placeholders** (`DemoAccountSeeder.java:62`):

```java
	@Override
	public void run(String... args) {
		List<Account> seeded = accounts.saveAll(OPENING_BALANCES.stream().map(Account::new).toList());

		log.info("Seeded {} demo accounts for the '{}' profile", seeded.size(), DEV_PROFILE);
	}
```

**Example 2 — error with the throwable as last arg** (`MockExchangeRateController.java:108`), and note the Javadoc explains *why the line exists*:

```java
	/**
	 * …
	 * <p>It is logged before it is swallowed. The response deliberately says nothing about
	 * what went wrong — a third party's would not — so without this line the one place the
	 * defect could be seen is the place that discards it.
	 */
	@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
	ResponseEntity<ProviderFault> anythingElse(Exception failure) {
		log.error("The stand-in FX provider failed to answer a request", failure);
		return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
				.body(new ProviderFault("rate_service_error", "The rate service failed to answer."));
	}
```

**Example 3 — the one place a different name is used** (`src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/ProblemDocumentAdvice.java:194`), inherited `logger` from `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`, string concatenation:

```java
		logger.error("Unhandled exception, answered as " + ProblemType.INTERNAL_ERROR.urn(), exception);
```

Message style: **sentence case, capital first letter, no trailing period, no prefixes/brackets/tags.** Values interpolated via `{}` (quoted with `'…'` when a string identifier). No log levels below `info` are used anywhere.

```java
	@Test
	@DisplayName("a claim is committed before the caller returns, and another connection sees it")
	void aClaimIsCommittedBeforeTheCallerReturns() throws SQLException {
		try (Connection onlooker = dataSource.getConnection()) {
			claims.claim(KEY, PAYLOAD_HASH);

			assertThat(readStatusThrough(onlooker)).isEqualTo("IN_PROGRESS");
		}

		assertThat(storedPayloadHash()).isEqualTo(PAYLOAD_HASH);
		assertThat(storedResponseBody()).isNull();
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("a second claim of a live key is refused by the constraint, not merged over it")
	void aSecondClaimOfALiveKeyIsRefusedByTheConstraint() {
		claims.claim(KEY, PAYLOAD_HASH);

		assertThatThrownBy(() -> claims.claim(KEY, A_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD_HASH))
				.isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
				.hasStackTraceContaining("IDEMPOTENCY_RECORDS_KEY_IS_UNIQUE");

		assertThat(storedPayloadHash()).isEqualTo(PAYLOAD_HASH);
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("the table refuses a status the domain has no name for")
	void refusesAStatusTheDomainHasNoNameFor() {
		assertThatThrownBy(() -> insertRecord("ABANDONED", null))
				.hasStackTraceContaining("IDEMPOTENCY_RECORDS_STATUS_IS_KNOWN");
	}

### Representative `@SpringBootTest` integration test — base class + scenario base + a test

`src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/testsupport/BootedApplicationTest.java` (full):

```java
package hu.bankmonitor.testsupport;

import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.server.LocalServerPort;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.client.RestTestClient;

/**
 * Base for tests that need the whole application running on a real port.
 *
 * <p>The configuration lives here rather than being repeated on each subclass for a
 * reason beyond tidiness: Spring caches one application context per distinct
 * configuration, so two classes differing by a single annotation pay two boots. Holding
 * the annotations in one place makes the shared context structural rather than a
 * coincidence the next edit could break.
 *
 * <p>{@code RANDOM_PORT} rather than MockMvc, because the claims these tests make are
 * about the servlet container itself — that a request reaches a listening socket, and
 * what kind of thread Tomcat serves it on. MockMvc would bypass it and prove neither.
 */
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(ThreadProbeController.class)
public abstract class BootedApplicationTest {

	@LocalServerPort
	private int port;

	/**
	 * A client bound to the running server. {@code TestRestTemplate} is gone in Spring
	 * Boot 4; {@code RestTestClient} is its Spring Framework 7 replacement.
	 */
	protected RestTestClient client() {
		return RestTestClient.bindToServer().baseUrl("http://localhost:" + port).build();
	}
}
```

Its Javadoc states the two rules that will bite the outbox tests:

> "**Nothing here is transactional, and that is the point.** A `@Transactional` test method makes every write it performs invisible to any other connection and rolls the lot back at the end … Every subclass needs real commits, so the price is paying for the cleanup by hand."
> "The tables are emptied before each method as well as after: one in-memory H2 database is shared by every test in the suite, whichever application context booted it."
> "Rows go in and come back out in SQL rather than through the entities, so what is asserted is what reached the database — a round trip through the mapping under test would agree with itself whatever it wrote."

And the concrete test, `src/test/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/transfers/EveryTransferOpensItsCheckLedgerTest.java`:

```java
class EveryTransferOpensItsCheckLedgerTest extends TransferScenario {

	private static final long SOURCE = 1L;
	private static final long DESTINATION = 2L;
	private static final long OPENING_BALANCE = 250_00L;

	@Autowired
	private CheckLedger ledger;

	@BeforeEach
	void openBothAccounts() {
		openAccount(SOURCE, OPENING_BALANCE, EUR);
		openAccount(DESTINATION, 0L, EUR);
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("requesting a Transfer opens one outstanding row per required Check")
	void opensOneOutstandingRowPerRequiredCheck() {
		Transfer requested = reservation.reserve(transferOf(80_00L, SOURCE, DESTINATION));

		assertThat(checkLedgerRows())
				.allSatisfy(row -> {
					assertThat(row).containsEntry("TRANSFER_ID", requested.getId());
					assertThat(row).containsEntry("VERDICT", null);
				})
				.extracting(row -> row.get("REQUIRED_CHECK"))
				.containsExactlyInAnyOrder("FRAUD", "MANUAL_APPROVAL");
	}

	@Test
	@DisplayName("a refused Transfer leaves no ledger behind either")
	void writesNoLedgerWhenTheTransferIsRefused() {
		assertThatThrownBy(() -> reservation.reserve(transferOf(OPENING_BALANCE + 1, SOURCE, DESTINATION)))
				.isInstanceOf(InsufficientFundsException.class);

		assertThat(transferRows()).isEmpty();
		assertThat(checkLedgerRows()).isEmpty();
	}
```

**This last one is the exact template for ticket 27's "an event written in a transaction that rolls back is never published".** Note the H2 column keys come back **UPPERCASE** (`"TRANSFER_ID"`, `"VERDICT"`).

There is no Mockito usage in any test read. Where a collaborator must be faked, a hand-written static nested `private static final class` implementing the package-private repository is used, e.g. `FakeLedgerRows implements CheckLedgerRepository` in `RecordingAVerdictAnswersOneOutstandingCheckTest`, with unsupported methods throwing `AssertionError`:

AssertJ throughout — static imports of `assertThat`, `assertThatThrownBy`, `assertThatCode` from `org.assertj.core.api.Assertions`. JUnit 5 (`@Test`, `@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`). No Hamcrest, no JUnit assertions.
